The Dedekind–MacNeille Completion of a Poset

The Dedekind–MacNeille completion (also called the normal completion) of a partially ordered set P is the smallest complete lattice L into which P embeds order‑preservingly. For each subset A ⊆ P define its lower set A↓ = {x ∈ P : x ≤ a for all a ∈ A} and its upper set A↑ = {x ∈ P : a ≤ x for all a ∈ A}. A cut of P is a pair (L, U) with L = U↓ and U = L↑. The set of all cuts ordered by (L₁, U₁) ≤ (L₂, U₂) iff L₁ ⊆ L₂ forms a complete lattice, the Dedekind–MacNeille completion DM(P). The embedding sends p ∈ P to the cut ({x : x ≤ p}, {x : p ≤ x}). This construction is functorial and yields a complete lattice that is join‑dense and meet‑dense in the image of P. If P is already a lattice, the embedding is a lattice homomorphism but need not be onto; the completion adds all missing joins and meets. The Dedekind–MacNeille completion of a distributive lattice is again distributive, and of a modular lattice is modular. However, the completion of a finite lattice can be infinite; for example, the poset of finite subsets of an infinite set ordered by inclusion has a completion isomorphic to the powerset lattice. The universal property: any order‑preserving map from P to a complete lattice C extends uniquely to a complete lattice homomorphism from DM(P) to C. This makes DM(P) the free complete lattice generated by P in the category of posets with order‑preserving maps. In domain theory, the ideal completion of a poset (the set of all directed lower sets) is a sublattice of the Dedekind–MacNeille completion and is often preferred because it preserves directed joins. The Dedekind–MacNeille completion is also the lattice of all Galois‑closed subsets of the formal context (P, P, ≤), linking it to formal concept analysis.

The Arguesian Identity and Modular Varieties

The Arguesian identity is a lattice‑theoretic formulation of Desargues' theorem from projective geometry. In a lattice L, the identity states that for all elements a₀, a₁, b₀, b₁, c₀, c₁ ∈ L, if (a₀ ∨ a₁) ∧ (b₀ ∨ b₁) ∧ (c₀ ∨ c₁) ≤ (a₀ ∨ b₀) ∧ (a₁ ∨ b₁) ∨ (a₀ ∨ c₀) ∧ (a₁ ∨ c₁) ∨ (b₀ ∨ c₀) ∧ (b₁ ∨ c₁) then a certain equality holds. Equivalently, a lattice satisfies the Arguesian law iff it can be embedded into the lattice of subspaces of a module over a ring (or a vector space over a division ring). This characterization is due to Jónsson and others. A variety of algebras is congruence‑modular iff the congruence lattice of every algebra in the variety satisfies the Arguesian identity. The Freese–McKenzie theorem (1987) shows that in any congruence‑modular variety, the commutator [α, β] of two congruences can be defined using the Arguesian law, yielding a deep structure theory analogous to group commutators. The Arguesian identity is strictly stronger than modularity; there are modular lattices that are not Arguesian (e.g., the lattice of submodules of a non‑Desarguesian projective plane). In a modular lattice, the Arguesian identity is equivalent to the condition that every sublattice generated by three elements is Arguesian. This property is crucial for the representation of modular lattices as submodule lattices and for the coordinatization theorem of von Neumann. The Arguesian law also appears in the study of linear logic and quantum logic, where the lattice of closed subspaces of a Hilbert space satisfies it. Understanding the Arguesian identity is essential for advanced work in universal algebra, lattice‑based cryptography, and the semantics of substructural logics.

Worked Example: Verifying the Arguesian Identity in a Submodule Lattice
Let V be a vector space over a field F, and let L = Sub(V) be the lattice of all subspaces ordered by inclusion. Take subspaces A₀, A₁, B₀, B₁, C₀, C₁ such that A₀ ⊆ A₁, B₀ ⊆ B₁, C₀ ⊆ C₁. Show that the Arguesian identity holds in L.
In Sub(V), join is subspace sum and meet is intersection. The Arguesian identity reduces to a known projective geometry statement: if two triangles are perspective from a point, they are perspective from a line. Because V is a vector space over a field, its projective geometry is Desarguesian, so the identity holds. Concretely, one can verify that for any vectors the required inclusion follows from the modular law and the fact that dimensions add correctly. The key step uses the modular identity (X ∨ Y) ∧ Z = X ∨ (Y ∧ Z) when X ≤ Z, which holds in Sub(V). By expanding both sides of the Arguesian inequality and applying modularity repeatedly, the two sides become equal. Hence Sub(V) satisfies the Arguesian identity.
Exam Strategy: Recognizing Arguesian Contexts
When a question asks whether a given lattice is Arguesian, first check if it is a submodule lattice of a module over a ring. If the lattice is known to be the congruence lattice of an algebra from a congruence‑modular variety, the answer is yes. If the lattice is merely modular but not known to be representable as submodules, the answer may be no; look for a counterexample such as the lattice of submodules of a non‑Desarguesian projective plane. Memorize the equivalence: Arguesian ⇔ embeddable into a submodule lattice ⇔ congruence lattice of a congruence‑modular variety.

Ideal Completion and Scott Domains

The ideal completion of a poset P is the set Idl(P) of all ideals (directed lower sets) of P, ordered by inclusion. An ideal I ⊆ P is a non‑empty subset such that (i) if x ∈ I and y ≤ x then y ∈ I, and (ii) for any x, y ∈ I there exists z ∈ I with x ≤ z and y ≤ z. Idl(P) is a directed‑complete partial order (dcpo): every directed subset of ideals has a join given by union. Moreover, Idl(P) is an algebraic lattice whose compact elements are precisely the principal ideals ↓p = {x ∈ P : x ≤ p} for p ∈ P. The embedding p ↦ ↓p is order‑preserving and reflects order. If P has finite joins, the embedding preserves them. The ideal completion is the free dcpo generated by P in the category of posets with Scott‑continuous maps. A Scott domain is an algebraic dcpo in which every element is the directed join of compact elements below it; equivalently, a Scott domain is (up to isomorphism) the ideal completion of a poset with a basis of compact elements. The way‑below relation x ≪ y in a Scott domain means that for every directed set D with sup D ≥ y, there exists d ∈ D with x ≤ d. In an algebraic lattice, c ≪ y iff c is compact and c ≤ y. The Scott topology on a dcpo has as open sets those upper sets U such that if sup D ∈ U for a directed D, then D ∩ U ≠ ∅. Scott domains provide the standard denotational models for the λ‑calculus and for programming languages with recursion. The Plotkin powerdomain, Hoare powerdomain, and Smyth powerdomain are constructed on Scott domains to model nondeterminism. The ideal completion also appears in formal concept analysis: the concept lattice of a formal context (G, M, I) is isomorphic to the ideal completion of the poset of formal concepts ordered by extent inclusion. Understanding the ideal completion is essential for domain theory, denotational semantics, and the theory of algebraic lattices.

Birkhoff's Representation Theorem for Finite Distributive Lattices

Birkhoff's representation theorem states that every finite distributive lattice L is isomorphic to the lattice of lower sets (order ideals) of its poset of join‑irreducible elements J(L), ordered by the induced order. An element j ∈ L is join‑irreducible if j ≠ 0 and whenever j = x ∨ y then j = x or j = y. In a finite distributive lattice, every element can be uniquely expressed as a join of join‑irreducible elements. The map φ: L → Idl(J(L)) defined by φ(x) = {j ∈ J(L) : j ≤ x} is a lattice isomorphism. Conversely, given any finite poset P, the lattice of its lower sets Idl(P) is a finite distributive lattice whose join‑irreducibles are the principal ideals ↓p. This establishes a categorical duality between the category of finite distributive lattices with lattice homomorphisms and the category of finite posets with order‑preserving maps. The theorem extends to infinite distributive lattices under the condition of complete distributivity and the existence of enough completely join‑irreducible elements (the Stone representation for Boolean algebras is a special case). In computer science, the theorem underlies the representation of data types as ideal completions of posets of finite approximations. In combinatorics, it connects distributive lattices to antichains and order polynomials. The number of elements in a finite distributive lattice equals the number of antichains in its poset of join‑irreducibles (Dedekind numbers for Boolean algebras). The theorem also yields a polynomial‑time algorithm for testing whether a given finite lattice is distributive: compute the poset of join‑irreducibles and verify that the lattice of its lower sets matches the original lattice. Birkhoff's representation is a cornerstone of lattice theory, linking algebraic structure to order‑theoretic structure.

Congruence Lattices and the Commutator in Universal Algebra

For an algebra A (a set equipped with operations), a congruence is an equivalence relation compatible with all operations. The set Con(A) of all congruences ordered by inclusion forms an algebraic lattice; its compact elements are the finitely generated congruences Θ(a, b) (the smallest congruence identifying a and b). In a congruence‑modular variety, the commutator [α, β] of two congruences α, β ∈ Con(A) is defined as the smallest congruence γ such that the quotient algebra A/γ satisfies a certain term condition (the “term condition” of Smith). The commutator measures how far α and β are from permuting; it satisfies [α, β] ≤ α ∧ β and is symmetric. In groups, the commutator of normal subgroups corresponds to the group commutator subgroup. In rings, it corresponds to the product of ideals. The commutator enables a deep structure theory: an algebra is abelian iff [1, 1] = 0, where 1 is the top congruence and 0 the bottom. A variety is congruence‑modular iff the commutator satisfies the “modular law” [α, β ∨ γ] = [α, β] ∨ [α, γ] when α ≤ γ. The Freese–McKenzie theorem characterizes modular congruence lattices by the Arguesian identity. The commutator also plays a central role in tame congruence theory (Hobby–McKenzie), which analyzes the local structure of finite algebras via minimal sets and types (unary, affine, Boolean, lattice, semilattice). The lattice of congruences of a finite algebra can be decomposed into a “semi‑lattice” of prime intervals, each labeled by a type. This theory has applications in constraint satisfaction problems (CSP) and in the classification of finite simple algebras. Understanding congruence lattices and the commutator is essential for advanced universal algebra, the algebraic approach to CSP, and the study of Maltsev conditions.

  • Confusing the Dedekind–MacNeille completion with the ideal completion; the former adds all cuts, the latter only directed lower sets.
  • Assuming every modular lattice satisfies the Arguesian identity; non‑Desarguesian projective planes give counterexamples.
  • Thinking that the way‑below relation coincides with the order relation in all dcpos; it is strictly finer and equals compact‑below only in algebraic lattices.
  • Misapplying Birkhoff's representation to infinite distributive lattices without checking complete distributivity and enough completely join‑irreducibles.
  • Believing the commutator [α, β] is always equal to α ∧ β; it is generally smaller and captures non‑abelian behavior.
  • Overlooking that the compact elements of Con(A) are exactly the finitely generated congruences, not all principal congruences.
  • Treating the Plotkin powerdomain as a lattice of all subsets rather than of non‑empty compact saturated convex sets.
